overview: The District of Columbia is a federal district rather than a state, and it is small and largely urban, so it is no surprise that our directory lists only a single named waterfall here, ranking it 48th among the states and districts covered. That one feature, Little Falls on the Potomac River, is nonetheless a direct expression of the region's geology. Washington sits on the fall line, the boundary where the hard, crystalline rocks of the Piedmont meet the softer sediments of the Atlantic Coastal Plain. Its waterfall story is therefore one of river geology and history rather than mountain scenery.

As the Potomac crosses that boundary, it tumbles over resistant rock in a series of rapids and ledges, from Great Falls upstream down to Little Falls near the District's northwestern edge. Below Little Falls the river becomes tidal, which is why the falls historically marked the upper limit of navigation and help explain why a capital city grew where it did. Little Falls is a stretch of rapids rather than a tall drop, best appreciated as part of the Potomac Gorge, one of the most geologically and ecologically distinctive river corridors in the eastern United States.

regions.name: Potomac Gorge and the Fall Line
regions.text: The District's waterfall country is the Potomac River corridor at its northwestern corner. Little Falls is a stretch of rapids where the river drops over bedrock ledges as it leaves the Piedmont, and it can be seen from the Chain Bridge, which crosses the Potomac just downstream. Rocky bluffs, floodplain forest and the remains of historic canal and water-supply works line this part of the river. The setting is shared with Maryland and Virginia, and the more famous Great Falls of the Potomac lies a short distance upstream outside the District. Water levels vary widely with rainfall upstream, and high flows turn the rapids into a powerful, churning chute.

bestTime: Little Falls changes character with the Potomac's flow rather than with any snowmelt calendar of its own. The river is typically highest in late winter and spring, when rain and melting snow across its large upstream basin swell the rapids; this is when the falls look most impressive from the Chain Bridge. Summer and early autumn usually bring lower water and more exposed rock, which shows the ledges and channels clearly. Thunderstorms and tropical systems can raise the river quickly at any time of year. Autumn color along the gorge, generally in late October and early November, makes for a pleasant visit, and weekday mornings are quieter on nearby trails and towpaths.
planning: Little Falls sits within a corridor of federal parkland, with the C&O Canal National Historical Park along the Maryland side of the river and other National Park Service land nearby, so trails, towpaths and viewpoints are generally public. Parking near the Chain Bridge and along the river is limited and fills on pleasant weekends; many visitors walk or bike in along the towpath or the Capital Crescent Trail. The main hazard is the river itself: the Potomac in this stretch has fast currents, strong undertows and submerged rocks, and drownings occur here. Stay out of the water, keep children close on the rocks, and be cautious after rain when the river rises.

faqs.q: Is Little Falls an actual waterfall?
faqs.a: It is a stretch of rapids and small drops where the Potomac crosses the fall line rather than a single tall cascade. It is the only named falls feature within the District in our directory.

faqs.q: Where is the best view of Little Falls?
faqs.a: The Chain Bridge, which crosses the Potomac just downstream, offers the most accessible view. For larger falls on the same river, Great Falls lies a short drive upstream in Maryland and Virginia.
